title.en: The sound of a far-away train

text.en: Have you ever lain awake and heard a train in the distance? Where did you imagine it was going? In this poem, Edna St. Vincent Millay writes about the pull of a train that is far away but always heard, and about her wish to ride any train, no matter where it goes.

You complete a word web on travel and imagine going to an adventure camp with your classmates and teacher, saying how you will travel, what you will take, why you want to go, what activities you would do and how long it will take. You also discuss why people enjoy train journeys.
The first stanza says the railroad track is miles away and the day is loud with voices, but the speaker still hears a train's whistle shrieking, though no train passes close by. The second stanza says that at night, though the night is still for sleep and dreaming, she sees the red cinders of the train against the sky and hears its engine steaming. The third stanza says her heart is warm with the friends she has, and she will never know better friends, yet she would take any train, no matter where it is going.
The main ideas are: stanza 1, she hears the train whistle during the day even though it is far away; stanza 2, at night she imagines the train and hears its engine in the quiet; stanza 3, she has a strong desire to take any train, wherever it goes. The rhyme scheme is ABAB in each stanza, for example away and day in the first stanza, and speaking and shrieking. The word shrieking gives human or animal qualities to the train's whistle, which is personification. The poet's tone is content and wistful, and the train symbolises adventure and opportunities. The line there isn't a train goes by is repeated in all stanzas to highlight the speaker's fascination with the train. Both the busy day and the still night have the train in common.
Imagery is descriptive language that creates mental pictures and appeals to the senses. Phrases such as day is loud, whistle shrieking, cinders red on the sky and engine steaming appeal to hearing and sight. The phrase cinders red on the sky tells us the train sends up glowing sparks that light the night sky. In the lines My heart is warm with the friends I make, warm means full of love, and the speaker says her friends are the best, so her tone is grateful and content. The line no matter where it is going shows her love of travel and adventure. The poet imagines the train rather than sees it, since it is miles away, so the poem is also about imagination and longing.
Matching expressions: miles away shows the distance of the train; cinders red shows the glow of sparks in the night sky; heart is warm shows affection for friends; day is loud shows the busy, noisy day; engine steaming shows the fast and powerful movement of the train. In the fill-in sentences, her heart is warm with the joy of rekindled memories, I could hear the engine steaming, the marketplace is loud with the chatter of shoppers, the bonfire threw cinders red into the sky, and the train could be heard miles away. Sound words for voices include shouting, yelling, screaming, screeching, bawling, sobbing and calling out. A shopkeeper might be yelling to attract customers, and a toddler bawling after dropping his ice cream.
In the announcement about a school trip to the National Science Centre, you circle the incorrect statements and then correct them after listening again. The letter c has two sounds, /k/ as in cat, and /s/ as in city. It sounds /s/ when it is followed by e, i or y, as in cinders, cell and cycle. In other cases, such as cat, cup and clap, it sounds /k/.

problem.en: Mark the rhyme scheme of the first stanza: away, speaking, day, shrieking.

text.en: Label the first line A.
Find matches.

why.en: Speaking is B, day matches away, and shrieking matches speaking, so the scheme is ABAB.

problem.en: Say the sound of c: cinders, cat.

text.en: Check the next letter.

why.en: Cinders has i after c, so it sounds s.

text.en: Cat has a.

prompt.en: Explain what the train means to the poet and how the poem shows it.

requiredIdeas.en: She hears the whistle by day and sees the glow by night even though the train is far away.
The train symbolises adventure and opportunity.
She would take any train no matter where it goes.
The poem uses imagery, repetition and personification.

commonMisconceptions.en: The poet is afraid of trains.
The poem is about a train accident.

points.en: Travel is a poem by Edna St. Vincent Millay about her wish to ride any train.
The whistle is heard by day and the glowing cinders are seen at night.
The rhyme scheme is ABAB, and the whistle is personified as shrieking.
Imagery and repetition show her fascination.
The letter c sounds /s/ before e, i or y and /k/ otherwise.
